title: Quotient coalgebra, induction and kernels for relative Hopf modules
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Let $H$ be a unital commutative $k$-algebra with algebra maps $\Delta:H\to H\otimes_kH$, $\epsilon:H\to k$ and $S:H\to H$ satisfying $(\Delta\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta$, $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta=1_H$, and $\mu(S\otimes1)\Delta=\mu(1\otimes S)\Delta=\eta\epsilon$, where $\mu$ and $\eta$ are multiplication and unit and tensor identifications are understood. Let $A\subseteq H$ be a unital $k$-subalgebra with $\Delta(A)\subseteq A\otimes_kH$. Module tensors have the meaning of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], and algebra tensors that of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. Put $A^+=\ker(\epsilon|_A)$ and let $J=HA^+$ be the ideal generated by $A^+$. Then $\epsilon(J)=0$ and $\Delta(J)\subseteq J\otimes_kH+H\otimes_kJ$, so $C=H/J$ is a coalgebra with quotient map $\pi$, comultiplication $\Delta_C\pi=(\pi\otimes\pi)\Delta$ and counit $\epsilon_C\pi=\epsilon$. Multiplication induces an $H$-action $h\cdot\pi(t)=\pi(ht)$ on $C$. A relative Hopf module $X$ means a left $H$-module with a $k$-linear map $\alpha_X:X\to C\otimes_kX$ satisfying $(\Delta_C\otimes1)\alpha_X=(1\otimes\alpha_X)\alpha_X$, $(\epsilon_C\otimes1)\alpha_X=1_X$, and $\alpha_X(hx)=\sum h_{(1)}\cdot x_{(-1)}\otimes h_{(2)}x_{(0)}$; subscripts denote finite tensor expansions of $\Delta(h)$ and $\alpha_X(x)$. Its coinvariants $R(X)=\{x\in X:\alpha_X(x)=\pi(1)\otimes x\}$ form an $A$-submodule. For every $A$-module $M$, $L(M)=H\otimes_AM$ is a relative Hopf module with $\alpha_{L(M)}(h\otimes m)=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes(h_{(2)}\otimes m)$, and $\eta_M(m)=1\otimes m$ belongs to $R(L(M))$. An $A$-linear map $f:M\to N$ induces a relative Hopf-module morphism $L(f)=1_H\otimes f$. Here a relative Hopf-module morphism is an $H$-linear map commuting with $\alpha$. If $u:X\to Y$ is any such morphism, its vector-space kernel $K$ is an $H$-submodule with a unique restricted coaction making the inclusion a relative Hopf-module morphism. Under this inclusion, $R(K)=K\cap R(X)$.

source.place: Bichon, arXiv:2301.05480v2, section 2.1, quotient coalgebra and induced relative Hopf modules; Theorem 2.1 discussion of underlying exact sequences, specialized to kernels over a field. Read at https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2; local PDF WANTED in report.md.

proof.text:
First record the quotient relation used below. For $a\in A$, $a-\epsilon(a)1\in A^+$, hence $\pi(ta)=\epsilon(a)\pi(t)$ for every $t\in H$, directly from $J=HA^+$. Choose a finite expression $\Delta(a)=\sum_i a_i\otimes t_i$ with $a_i\in A$, using the right coideal hypothesis. The counit identity gives $a=\sum_i\epsilon(a_i)t_i$. Consequently
$$\Delta(a)=1\otimes a+\sum_i(a_i-\epsilon(a_i)1)\otimes t_i,$$
with each $a_i-\epsilon(a_i)1\in A^+$. Tensor multiplication is componentwise by the cited algebra-tensor statement; the equalities here use only bilinearity and the given counit axiom.

source.place: Bichon arXiv:2301.05480v2, §2.1, explicit verification of the preliminary constructions; HTML https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2 read 2026-10-24; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text:
For $a\in A^+$ and $h\in H$, multiplicativity gives $\epsilon(ha)=0$ and
$$\Delta(ha)=\Delta(h)(1\otimes a)+\sum_i\Delta(h)((a_i-\epsilon(a_i)1)\otimes t_i).$$
The first term belongs to $H\otimes_kJ$ and every summand of the second belongs to $J\otimes_kH$, by expanding $\Delta(h)$ into pure tensors. Every element of $J$ is a finite sum of such $ha$, so linearity proves both asserted coideal inclusions. Here these tensor subspaces mean images of their inclusion maps; this argument itself needs no exactness theorem.

proof.text: The maps $(\pi\otimes\pi)\Delta$ and $\epsilon$ kill $J$ by step 2, hence descend uniquely to linear maps $\Delta_C:C\to C\otimes_kC$ and $\epsilon_C:C\to k$ on the quotient vector space. On every representative $\pi(h)$, the two triple comultiplications are the images under $\pi\otimes\pi\otimes\pi$ of $(\Delta\otimes1)\Delta(h)$ and $(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta(h)$; they agree. The two counit composites on $\pi(h)$ equal $\pi(h)$ by the counit axioms of $H$. Surjectivity of $\pi$ proves the coalgebra laws. The action $h\pi(t)=\pi(ht)$ is well defined since $hJ\subseteq J$, and its unit and associativity are those of multiplication in $H$. In particular $e=\pi(1)$ satisfies $\Delta_C(e)=e\otimes e$ and $\epsilon_C(e)=1$, since $\Delta$ and $\epsilon$ preserve units.

source.place: Bichon arXiv:2301.05480v2, §2.1, explicit verification of the preliminary constructions; HTML https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2 read 2026-10-24; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text:
The coinvariants are the kernel of the linear map $x\mapsto\alpha_X(x)-e\otimes x$, so form a vector subspace. For $x\in R(X)$ and $a\in A$, write $\Delta(a)=\sum_i a_i\otimes t_i$ as in step 1. Compatibility of the relative coaction and the quotient relation of step 1 give
$$\alpha_X(ax)=\sum_i\pi(a_i)\otimes t_ix=\sum_i\epsilon(a_i)e\otimes t_ix=e\otimes ax.$$
Thus the subspace is stable under $A$, with the restricted action, as required.

proof.text:
For $M$ an $A$-module put $L(M)=H\otimes_AM$ with $H$ acting on the first factor. Define on pairs
$$\beta(h,m)=\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes(h_{(2)}\otimes_A m).$$
It is additive and $k$-bilinear. For $a\in A$ write $\Delta(a)=\sum_i a_i\otimes t_i$ with $a_i\in A$. Then step 1 and the counit identity give
$$\beta(ha,m)=\sum_{(h),i}\epsilon(a_i)\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes(h_{(2)}t_i\otimes_A m)=\sum_{(h)}\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes(h_{(2)}a\otimes_A m)=\beta(h,am).$$
With $A$ acting on the last tensor factor, this also gives $\beta(ha,m)=a\beta(h,m)$ and $\beta(h,am)=a\beta(h,m)$. The tensor universal property therefore produces the claimed linear coaction $\alpha_{L(M)}$. The $H$-action on $L(M)$ respects the balancing relation because $H$ is commutative.

proof.text:
Check the relative Hopf-module identities on the spanning tensors $h\otimes_A m$. The two coassociativity composites are respectively
$$\sum\pi(h_{(1)(1)})\otimes\pi(h_{(1)(2)})\otimes(h_{(2)}\otimes_A m),\qquad \sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes\pi(h_{(2)(1)})\otimes(h_{(2)(2)}\otimes_A m),$$
which agree by coassociativity of $H$. The counit composite is $\sum\epsilon(h_{(1)})(h_{(2)}\otimes_A m)=h\otimes_A m$. For $g\in H$, multiplicativity of $\Delta$ gives
$$\alpha_{L(M)}(gh\otimes_A m)=\sum\pi(g_{(1)}h_{(1)})\otimes(g_{(2)}h_{(2)}\otimes_A m)=\sum g_{(1)}\cdot\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes g_{(2)}(h_{(2)}\otimes_A m),$$
exactly the compatibility identity. Linearity extends these identities to every element.

source.place: Bichon arXiv:2301.05480v2, §2.1, explicit verification of the preliminary constructions; HTML https://arxiv.org/html/2301.05480v2 read 2026-10-24; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Since $\Delta(1)=1\otimes1$, $\alpha_{L(M)}(1\otimes_A m)=e\otimes(1\otimes_A m)$, proving the unit's coinvariance. The map $m\mapsto1\otimes_A m$ is $A$-linear since $1\otimes_A am=a\otimes_A m=a(1\otimes_A m)$. For an $A$-linear $f:M\to N$, the tensor universal property defines $L(f)(h\otimes_A m)=h\otimes_A f(m)$. It is $H$-linear by multiplication on $h$, and both sides of its coaction square send $h\otimes_A m$ to $\sum\pi(h_{(1)})\otimes(h_{(2)}\otimes_A f(m))$. Thus $L(f)$ is a relative Hopf-module morphism.

proof.text: Let $K=\ker(u)$ and $i:K\hookrightarrow X$. Since $u$ is $H$-linear, $u(hx)=hu(x)=0$ for $x\in K$, so $K$ is an $H$-submodule. The vector space $C$ is flat by the cited field-flatness statement. Apply the cited flat tensor exactness to $0\to K\xrightarrow{i}X\xrightarrow{u}Y$ over $k$. It says that $1_C\otimes i$ is injective with image $\ker(1_C\otimes u)$. The morphism identity gives $(1_C\otimes u)\alpha_X i=\alpha_Yui=0$. Therefore there is a unique linear map $\alpha_K:K\to C\otimes_kK$ with $(1_C\otimes i)\alpha_K=\alpha_Xi$: each value is the unique preimage in that image. Additivity and scalar linearity follow by uniqueness. This constructs the restricted coaction without assuming flatness of $H$ over $A$.

source.place: Tag 00HD, lemma-flat, and Tag 00HB, definition-flat; vector-space freeness: fields.tex, Tag 09FN, lemma-vector-space-is-free; application to the kernel assertion in Bichon §2.1, Theorem 2.1 discussion.

proof.text: For coassociativity of $\alpha_K$, compare its two composites after $1_C\otimes1_C\otimes i$. Naturality of tensor maps and the defining equality of step 8 turn them into $(\Delta_C\otimes1_X)\alpha_Xi$ and $(1_C\otimes\alpha_X)\alpha_Xi$, which agree. The comparison map is injective: apply the cited field-flatness and tensor-exactness statements with $C\otimes_kC$ and the injection $i$. The counit equation follows after the injective map $i$, since $i(\epsilon_C\otimes1_K)\alpha_K=(\epsilon_C\otimes1_X)\alpha_Xi=i$. Finally, compare $\alpha_K(hx)$ with $\sum h_{(1)}\cdot x_{(-1)}\otimes h_{(2)}x_{(0)}$ after $1_C\otimes i$. The first image is $\alpha_X(hi(x))$; the second is the same by compatibility on $X$ and $H$-linearity of $i$. Injectivity from step 8 proves equality. Thus $K$ is a relative Hopf module, and $i$ is a morphism; any restricted coaction must satisfy the same equation, so step 8 proves uniqueness.

source.place: Tag 00HD, lemma-flat, and Tag 00HB, definition-flat; vector-space freeness: fields.tex, Tag 09FN, lemma-vector-space-is-free; application to the kernel assertion in Bichon §2.1, Theorem 2.1 discussion.

proof.text: For $x\in K$, the equality $\alpha_K(x)=e\otimes x$ implies $\alpha_X(i(x))=e\otimes i(x)$ by step 8. Conversely, that equality in $C\otimes_kX$ implies the equality in $C\otimes_kK$ by injectivity of $1_C\otimes i$ already proved in step 8. Hence under the inclusion $i$, the coinvariants of $K$ are exactly $K\cap R(X)$, with the inherited $A$-module structure. This is the final assertion.
